name: American Red Cross: Measles & Rubella Partnership mobilisation (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: household visits before measles-rubella campaigns through the Measles & Rubella Partnership; the Red Cross publishes no list of the year's countries, so the partnership countries where its volunteers' visits are documented (Kenya, Nigeria, Malawi, Mozambique) share equally (a judgment).
summary: Through the Measles & Rubella Partnership the American Red Cross funds Red Cross and Red Crescent volunteers who visit households before vaccination campaigns to bring children in (3 million households in its fiscal year to June 2025, the latest audited year: the FY2026 accounts weren't on the Red Cross's financials page on 4 November 2026). This model counts the measles deaths averted among the few extra children vaccinated because of a visit, in years of healthy life per $1,000, at about 8% of the international programme's spending (the measles grants' share of its grants abroad in the Form 990). Nothing in the chain is measured for this programme: the extra vaccinations per visit (a Kenyan Red Cross survey's 26% of children who would have missed the dose, discounted to about 3%), the deaths each averts and the programme's spending are wide judgments, so the result is mostly uncertainty and the model is discounted for missing data. It is below the site's global-health median because most children would have been vaccinated without a visit, so the Red Cross's cost per extra child vaccinated is about $45, and the dose protects a child for only the two years or so left under five, often on top of an earlier dose.

So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

Households visited to encourage measles and rubella vaccination, FY2025

source.title: American Red Cross, Annual Report, Fiscal Year 2025 (July 2024 - June 2025)
source.quote: MORE THAN 3 million households visited to encourage vaccinations through the Measles & Rubella Partnership.

rows.explainer: Volunteers going door to door before and during campaigns; the Red Cross's own count.

rows.label: Children under five per household visited
rows.explainer: In Kenya's 2012 campaign, Red Cross volunteers counted 161,695 eligible children aged 9-59 months in the 164,643 households they visited, 0.98 a household (Mbabazi et al. 2014, Health Policy and Planning): volunteers target households with young children. The national average (DHS household sizes of 4.2-4.6 with about 15% under five) is about 0.7, the low end. Children 5-14 also get campaign doses, but their measles death risk is a small fraction of under-fives' and the rate below is per unvaccinated under-five, so they are counted in unmodelled benefits.

rows.label: Children under five in the households visited
rows.explainer: Every child under five in a visited household; the share vaccinated only because of the visit is the counterfactual adjustment.

rows.label: Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context: cost per child in a visited household, well under a dollar.

rows.label: Years under five left for a child vaccinated in the campaign
rows.explainer: Campaigns vaccinate children from 9 to 59 months; spread evenly over that span a child is on average 2.9 years old (the midpoint of 0.75 and 5), leaving 2.1 years before turning five, when the death rate below applies. From 1.5 (older children brought in) to 2.8 (younger).

rows.label: Measles deaths worldwide, 2023

source.title: WHO, news release, 14 November 2024: Measles cases surge worldwide, infecting 10.3 million people in 2023
source.quote: an estimated 107 500 people, mostly children younger than 5 years of age, died due to measles in 2023

rows.explainer: WHO and CDC's estimate, mostly children under five.

rows.label: Children who missed their first measles dose, 2023

source.title: WHO, news release, 14 November 2024: Measles cases surge worldwide, infecting 10.3 million people in 2023
source.quote: more than 22 million children missed their first dose of measles vaccine in 2023

rows.explainer: A yearly cohort of unvaccinated infants (WUENIC).

rows.label: Yearly cohorts of unvaccinated children under five at risk at once
rows.explainer: Each year's missed cohort stays unvaccinated through early childhood until a campaign or a late dose reaches it, so the unvaccinated under-fives alive at once are about four cohorts, from three (frequent campaigns) to six (under five's full span, few catch-ups).

rows.label: Measles death risk where the visits happen, relative to the world's unvaccinated children
rows.explainer: Measles death risk per unvaccinated child where the visits happen, relative to the world's. The WHO African region had 71% of the world's measles deaths in 2023 (75,942 of 107,482: Minta et al. 2024, MMWR) at 70% first-dose coverage, which with about 38 million surviving infants is about 11 million of the 22 million children who missed their first dose (about half): a relative risk of about 0.71 / 0.51 = 1.4. From 0.8 (Kenya, Malawi and Mozambique have lower measles mortality than the region's worst settings) to 2.5 (outbreak settings like northern Nigeria). The FY2025 campaign list by country isn't published.

source.title: Minta et al. (2024), Progress Toward Measles Elimination, Worldwide, 2000-2023, MMWR 73(45):1036-1042
source.page: Table 2: African Region, 75,942 estimated measles deaths in 2023 (71% of 107,482)
source.quote: Estimated measles deaths decreased 8%, from 116,800 in 2022 to 107,500 in 2023

rows.label: Share of measles deaths that are of children under five
rows.explainer: The site's shared share of measles deaths under five in sub-Saharan Africa (GBD, @death_ages.measles_ssa_share_under5), where all four countries of the visits are; WHO says the world's deaths are 'mostly children younger than 5 years of age'.

rows.label: Share of under-five measles deaths that are of unvaccinated children aged 9-59 months
rows.explainer: The rate below is per unvaccinated child, so the deaths of vaccinated children (vaccine failures) and of infants under 9 months, too young for the campaign, come out of the numerator. In the WHO African region, 'reported measles cases occurred among children aged 9–59 months, 79% of whom were either unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status' (Masresha et al. 2017, Progress toward measles elimination, African Region 2013-2016, MMWR 66(17); an upper bound, 'unknown' includes some vaccinated), and 9-59-month-olds are about 87% of under-five cases: about 0.7. Low end: 58-60% zero-dose among confirmed cases in Nigeria (NCDC 2020, Anambra 2011-2016).

rows.label: Yearly risk of dying of measles for an unvaccinated child
rows.explainer: Under-five measles deaths of unvaccinated children over the unvaccinated under-fives at risk, at the campaign settings' relative risk.

rows.label: Measles death risk over the protected years relative to the average unvaccinated under-five's
rows.explainer: The rate is an average over unvaccinated children under five, but the years a campaign dose protects fall mostly at ages 3-5 (about 3.6 on average, against about 2.9 for the children at risk), and measles mortality falls with age through early childhood (case fatality is highest in the second year of life, and older unvaccinated children are more often already immune from infection). About 0.8, from 0.6 to 1. Reference class: GBD 2021 measles deaths in Bauchi, Nigeria (the site's facts @givewell_common.measles_mortalities_per_year_among_people_under_age_1 and measles_both_under_5_2021) put ages 1-4 at about 0.92 of the under-five average per cohort-year; the protected years are older still (3-5), so lower: 0.8.

rows.label: Reduction in measles deaths for a vaccinated child
rows.explainer: Reduction in an unvaccinated child's measles death risk from the campaign dose. Campaigns dose every child in the age band whatever their history: for a child never vaccinated, a dose at 12 months or older protects 92%; for one who had a routine dose at 9 months, the campaign dose only adds the second dose's protection over the first (94.1% − 77.0%); for one who had two already, nothing. Weighted by the zero-dose and two-dose shares: about 0.45. The site's shared GiveWell figure (@givewell_common.measles_vaccine_efficacy_rate_from_uzicanin_and_zimmerm, 0.73) is for an infant's dose at 9 months, the wrong age for campaign children, so it isn't used.
rows.formula: msl_zero_dose_share * msl_ve_one_dose_12m + (1 - msl_zero_dose_share) * (1 - msl_prior_two_dose_share) * max(0, msl_ve_two_dose - msl_ve_one_dose_9_11m)

rows.label: Share of the extra children vaccinated who had no measles dose before
rows.explainer: Routine first-dose coverage is about 85-90% in Kenya, Malawi and Mozambique and about 60% in Nigeria (WHO/UNICEF estimates), so about a fifth of children in the four countries have no dose; the children a visit brings in are the ones who would otherwise be missed, and those cluster among the zero-dose (households that miss routine visits miss campaigns too). About twice the average: 0.4, from 0.25 to 0.65.

rows.label: Of the extra children who had a dose before, share who already had two
rows.explainer: Second-dose coverage is roughly 40-75% across the four countries (WHO/UNICEF estimates), but the children a visit brings in are the hard to reach (in Anambra, Nigeria, 3.8% of cases had two doses against 34% with one): about 25%, from 10 to 40%. For them the campaign dose adds almost nothing.

rows.label: Measles vaccine effectiveness, one dose at 12 months or older

source.title: Uzicanin and Zimmerman (2011), Field effectiveness of live attenuated measles-containing vaccines: a review of published literature, J Infect Dis 204 Suppl 1:S133-48 (abstract)
source.quote: For a single dose of vaccine administered at 9-11 months of age and ≥12 months, the median VE was 77.0% (interquartile range [IQR], 62%-91%) and 92.0% (IQR, 86%-96%), respectively.

rows.explainer: Median of the published field estimates; estimates are generally lower in the African and South-East Asian regions, which the evidence adjustment allows for. Range: the review's interquartile range.

rows.label: Measles vaccine effectiveness, one dose at 9-11 months

source.title: Uzicanin and Zimmerman (2011), J Infect Dis 204 Suppl 1 (abstract)
source.quote: For a single dose of vaccine administered at 9-11 months of age and ≥12 months, the median VE was 77.0% (interquartile range [IQR], 62%-91%) and 92.0% (IQR, 86%-96%), respectively.

rows.explainer: The protection a child with a routine dose at 9 months already has. Range: the review's interquartile range.

rows.label: Measles vaccine effectiveness, two doses

source.title: Uzicanin and Zimmerman (2011), J Infect Dis 204 Suppl 1 (abstract)
source.quote: For 2 doses of measles-containing vaccine, compared with no vaccination, the median VE was 94.1% (IQR, 88.3%-98.3%).

rows.explainer: With the campaign dose as the second. Range: the review's interquartile range.

rows.label: Deaths caused indirectly, per direct death averted (immune amnesia in unmodelled benefits)
rows.explainer: 0: herd protection and the deaths after measles (immune amnesia) are in unmodelled benefits.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The unvaccinated child's yearly measles death risk, adjusted to the ages the protection covers, × the campaign dose's reduction × the years left under five.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: 1: the chain counts only under-fives.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Not used: the chain counts only under-fives (older children are in unmodelled benefits).

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Not used: the chain counts only under-fives (older children are in unmodelled benefits).

rows.label: Illness averted, as a share of the mortality and income benefits
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared supplementary share for illness averted by vaccines.

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: congenital rubella syndrome and the stillbirths it causes are in unmodelled benefits.

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person reached, ln(consumption) per year
rows.explainer: 0: no later-life income gain is modelled for measles vaccination.

rows.label: Years until the income gain starts
rows.explainer: Not used: there is no income gain.

rows.label: Years the long-term income gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a long-term income gain lasts (GiveWell's working years, 40), read by every model that counts one (INV-13).

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person reached, present value
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate, the wait included, so the result moves with it. Never type in a present value worked out elsewhere: rebuild it from its inputs.

rows.label: Resource sharing within households (multiplier on an earner's gain)
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (GiveWell's): an earner's income gain is shared with the household, so it counts this many times. Read by every model that values a long-term income gain (INV-13).

rows.label: Internal validity of the chain
rows.explainer: Only two doubts are left here: field vaccine effectiveness is generally lower in the African region than the review's medians (Uzicanin and Zimmerman 2011), and the death rate rests on modelled global estimates (WHO, GBD). The visit's effect carries its own self-report discount (msl_report_to_behaviour), so it isn't discounted again. 0.85, from 0.75 to 0.95.

rows.label: External validity: the trials' setting against this program's, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The settings' risk is in msl_setting_risk, so nothing is left to transfer (1); the low end for campaigns unlike the studies' routine programmes.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: The product of its two parts.

rows.label: Share of the children vaccinated only because of the visit
rows.explainer: The share of the children in visited households vaccinated in the campaign only because of the visit: the share whose carers said they would likely have missed the dose without the visit, times the share of those who really would have. Cross-checks from the research: home visits and village health education raise routine coverage where it is low (Cochrane, Oyo-Ita et al. 2023 update: health education risk ratio 1.36 for DTP3, low certainty); measles strategies in low- and middle-income countries raise coverage by a risk ratio of 1.19 (1.10-1.27: Yitbarek et al. 2025, BMJ Global Health); campaigns with strong mobilisation reach 92-96% (92% finger-mark confirmed in Mbabazi's districts; 95% nationally in Kenya's 2016 measles-rubella campaign, Subaiya et al. 2018, PLoS ONE), so the visit's gain on top of other mobilisation is a few points. About 3%, from 1 to 10%.

rows.label: Children whose carers said they would likely have missed the campaign dose without the visit

source.title: Mbabazi et al. (2014), Innovations in communication technologies for measles supplemental immunization activities: lessons from Kenya measles vaccination campaign, November 2012, Health Policy and Planning 30(5):638-44
source.quote: Twenty-five per cent of households were likely to miss the measles supplemental dose if they had not been reassured by the house visit.

rows.explainer: Kenya Red Cross volunteers' house visits before the 2012 campaign, 164,643 households in 11 urban districts: a quarter of households (26% of the children, the share used here, per the paper's results) said they would likely have missed the dose. Self-reported after the visit with no control group, so an upper bound on the visit's effect, taken down in the next row. The quote gives households; the paper's results give 26% of the children.

rows.label: Of those, the share who really would have missed the dose
rows.explainer: Carers reassured by a visit overstate what it changed, most would have heard of the campaign from radio, posters or neighbours, and the urban Kenyan settlements were harder to reach than most. Floor: in Benin's 2019 campaign, volunteers turned 751 of 862 refusing households (of about 300,000 visited) into acceptors (Aholoukpe and Davis 2020, Pan African Medical Journal), 0.25% of households from refusals alone. About an eighth, giving 3% of children (1-10%). This row carries all of the self-report discount; the evidence adjustment doesn't repeat it.

rows.label: Red Cross cost per extra child vaccinated (US$)
rows.explainer: The programme's full cost over the children vaccinated only because of a visit.

rows.label: Others' cost of vaccinating a child found by a visit (US$)
rows.explainer: What governments, Gavi, UNICEF and WHO spend to give one more child a measles-rubella campaign dose: the vaccine and injection supplies (about $1 a dose) plus the campaign's operational cost per child (a dollar or two). About $3, from $1 (the campaign runs anyway and one more child adds only a dose) to $8 (hard-to-reach areas). GiveWell's Gavi figure (@givewell_common.gavi_costs_incurred_per_child_counterfactually_vaccinat, about $29) covers a full routine schedule, not one campaign dose, so it is not used.

rows.label: Volunteer-days per household visited
rows.explainer: In Kenya 2012, 1,952 volunteers worked three days before and up to four days after the campaign for 164,643 households (Mbabazi et al. 2014): about 0.08 volunteer-days a household. From 0.04 (pre-campaign visits only) to 0.15 (sparse rural households).

rows.label: Value of a volunteer-day at local wages, net of stipends the grants pay (US$)
rows.explainer: A day's unskilled wage in Kenya, Nigeria, Malawi and Mozambique is a few dollars; national societies' volunteers often get a small stipend from the grant, which is already the Red Cross's cost. About $5 of unpaid value a day, from 0 (stipends cover it) to 8.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: The Red Cross's cost per extra child against everyone's: the vaccine and campaign (others' cost) and the national societies' volunteers' unpaid time (Convention 2). It follows the chain: fewer extra children per visit means a larger share of a smaller result.
rows.formula: msl_cost_per_extra_child / (msl_cost_per_extra_child + msl_others_cost_per_child + msl_households_visited * msl_volunteer_days_per_household * msl_volunteer_day_value / (people_reached * counterfactual_adj))

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: Visits reported that didn't happen or reached no one at home.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Other mobilisers for the same campaigns (governments, UNICEF) are in the counterfactual and funging inside the Red Cross in unmodelled benefits, as in the relief model; only outside effects are left: the visits draw in government campaign effort (above 1) or let another funder give less (below 1). 1, from 0.95 to 1.05.

source.title: The American National Red Cross, Consolidated Financial Statements, June 30, 2025 (audited by KPMG)
source.page: p. 24, note 7, Net assets with donor restrictions (in thousands)

rows.explainer: International gifts given and not yet spent at year end.

rows.label: Net assets restricted to international services, 30 June 2024 (US$)

source.title: The American National Red Cross, Consolidated Financial Statements, June 30, 2025 (audited by KPMG)
source.page: p. 24, note 7, Net assets with donor restrictions (in thousands)

rows.explainer: The same balance a year earlier, so the wait uses the average stock over the year, as the relief model does.

rows.label: Years a donation waits before the charity spends it
rows.explainer: Funds held (the average of the year-start and year-end balances) over a year's international spending: about a year, as in the relief model.

rows.label: Years from the charity's spending to the intervention reaching people
rows.explainer: Visits come in the weeks before a campaign; a few months from grant to campaign.

rows.label: Years from delivery to the middle of the protection
rows.explainer: Half the years of protection: the measles deaths averted come over childhood, discounted from the middle.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the benefits come
rows.explainer: Every wait is discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit (the income gain's own wait is counted from delivery, in ln_income_gain_per_person).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: the households visited are the Red Cross's own count, but the extra children vaccinated per visit, the measles death risk where the visits happen, the zero-dose share and the programme's spending are judgments anchored on research on other delivery (the Cochrane review of coverage interventions, a meta-analysis of measles vaccination strategies, a Kenyan Red Cross survey without a control group); the Red Cross publishes no comparison of coverage in visited and unvisited areas. So the shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above, the wait and the missing-data step included.

rows.label: Treatment costs averted, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared share for treatment costs averted.

rows.label: Rebound malaria from lost immunity, as a share of value lost
rows.explainer: 0: a vaccine doesn't weaken natural immunity the way malaria prevention does.

rows.label: Investment of income increases, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared share for income invested by families of children who survive.

rows.label: Other benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Older children vaccinated in the campaigns (+), rubella and congenital rubella syndrome averted (+), herd protection of unvisited children (+), deaths after measles from weakened immunity (+), other services promoted at the visits (+); against them, funging inside the Red Cross (restricted international gifts may let it move its own funds to domestic work: about −3%, 0 to −5%).

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: GiveWell-style supplementary adjustments, each its own row, summed: they add to the modelled value as one share, as in GiveWell's sheets.

Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights for the age band of each death averted (under five, 5–14, 15–49, 50 and over), times your multiplier on the value of a life: the site's one value of a death (docs/normalization.md 2.7).

rows.label: Units of value from deaths averted
Units of value from stillbirths averted
rows.explainer: A stillbirth averted at the site's one value (@givewell_shared.uov_per_stillbirth, GiveWell's), times your multiplier on the value of a life.

Units of value from illness averted
rows.explainer: A share of the deaths' and income's value, the base GiveWell's supplementary share has.

rows.label: Illness averted per person reached, in DALYs (before adjustments)

rows.label: Illness averted, in DALYs
Illness averted, in units of value
rows.explainer: The bridge from DALYs into units of value: the unit's conversion cancels it, so illness counts as healthy years whatever "Healthy year vs doubled-income year" is set to.

rows.label: Total units of value
rows.explainer: Illness and the other supplementary shares add to the modelled value side by side, as one sum of shares does in GiveWell's sheets; illness counted in DALYs comes in through its bridge.
